claims.statement: For NIC deployment and subnet joining, the source describes Actions-service Azure subscription RBAC permissions; listing permissions is not evidence of actual grants or least-privilege approval.
GitHub.Network permission inventory includes operations read, networkSettings read/write/delete and RegisteredSubscriptions read.
Microsoft.Network location permissions cover operations, operationResults and usages read; NIC permissions cover read/write/delete and join/action.
Network permissions include NSG join/read; public IP read/write/join; route-table join; VNET read and subnet join/read/write, preserving the source's publicIp/publicIP casing distinction.
Service association link permissions cover delete/read/write/details-read/validate; resource-group read and deployment read/write/operations-read plus deployment status read are listed.

Two tenant enterprise applications are named after configuration: GitHub CPS Network Service (85c49807-809d-4249-86e7-192762525474) and GitHub Actions API (4435c199-c3da-46b9-a61d-76de3f2c9f82); these public IDs are not proof of tenant installation.
The source script proposes one resource group, filled placeholders and Bash/WSL execution from the Bicep file directory; Azure location name is distinct from display name. Script is not executed.

Creating network settings adds a protective service association link; existing-subnet adaptation says connected NICs must first be deleted or SAL application fails. This destructive source prerequisite is not authorization.

The example registers GitHub.Network, creates group/NSG/VNET/subnet/settings and delegates subnet; set -e, conditional enterprise/organization database ID, API 2024-04-02 and adjustable example address prefixes are source-specific inputs, not target policy.

The example sequences login, subscription selection, provider registration, group creation, Bicep deployment, VNET creation, subnet delegation/NSG and settings creation using subnetId/businessId. Each command is prefixed '. az', a shell source-operator pattern requiring execution review, not a verified working Azure CLI recipe.

Cleanup is printed with echo rather than executed. GitHubId returned from the created settings resource is needed for GitHub network configuration; the CLI uses a selected query despite prose claiming a full payload. No live creation receipt exists.
Configure Azure resources before creating the GitHub private network configuration; troubleshooting navigation is conditional enterprise-cloud versus organization content, not implicit linked review.

Network configurations are organization-level outside GHEC and enterprise or organization level within GHEC; initial GHEC Azure setup uses enterprise slug/databaseId, with organization configurations only after enterprise setup and policy enablement.

Associating a network configuration grants every runner in its group access to the underlying VNET; Azure resources must be configured first. Group-wide reach is not per-runner consent or observed enforcement.

SAL prevents accidental subnet deletion; delete GitHub network configuration before network settings, whose deletion removes SAL, then delete subnet. Ordered conditional removal is source evidence, not authorized cleanup.
Navigation differs enterprise versus organization; open the intended Hosted compute networking configuration and review dependent runner groups before Delete configuration.

Deletion examples select a subscription and remove the identified GitHub.Network/networkSettings resource with API version, followed by subnet deletion. Target variables and external Azure procedures require separate authorization and review.
Enterprise organizations by default inherit enterprise network configurations and cannot create new ones; enterprise owners may enable independent organization configurations through policy.
Troubleshooting conditionally includes enterprise policy and supported regions, and requires configuring Azure before GitHub. Region include resolution remains separate.
Required outbound GitHub/Actions connectivity failure prevents bringing runners online and jobs being picked up, with VNetInjectionFailedToConnectToInternet; source directs reviewing Azure setup.

Subscription/resource-group locks may prevent NIC creation (no jobs) or deletion (address exhaustion or long QTA), with RunnerDeploymentScopeLocked. Removing locks or changing subnet is a source remedy needing security review, not adopted bypass.

Resource policies such as tags/names may block NIC creation and jobs, with RunnerDeploymentBlockedByPolicy; source proposes removing policy or using another subnet, not blanket authorization to weaken security.

Each runner consumes an IP; source links scale errors and reduced concurrency/high QTA to full subnet, with VNetInjectionSubnetIsFull, suggesting subnet enlargement or lower maximum concurrency. The source's maximum-runner wording is preserved, not silently repaired.
SAL may block deletion; a read example locates settings by subnetId using the creation API version and placeholder Entra bearer token. No credential acquired or command executed.

Complex proxies/firewalls may block agent readiness or anti-abuse tooling; source proposes a diagnostic VM/self-hosted runner, on a similar subnet if SAL prevents same-subnet deployment. Provisioning remains approval-gated.

Payload validation needs correct API version and businessId; HttpRequestPayloadAPISpecValidationFailed is shown. Source spells diagnostic option ---debug with three hyphens; this is an unresolved example defect, not verified CLI syntax.
Wrong organization databaseId instead of enterprise ID can bind settings to the wrong entity; source suggests delete/recreate with enterprise ID, which remains destructive and approval-gated.

Preview failover transition may run both networks simultaneously; approximately fifteen minutes is source testing, not SLA. Keep both accessible, verify Azure resources/configuration/runner-group association and sufficient failover IP capacity.

A GitHub-initiated failover heading offers Disable failover VNET to return to primary; verify primary health/access and regional outages. This must be reconciled with another fragment's manual-switch description, not assumed automatic failover proof.

Multiple VNET subnets and runner groups support private/on-premises resource access without opening internet ports, outbound policy control and connectivity log monitoring; these are capabilities, not observed configuration or enabled logs.

Source describes a runner NIC in the user's VNET and runner in the subnet region; Azure allows same-VNET inbound by default, GitHub cannot block it and requires no inbound connections. Explicit all-inbound blocking is recommended, not a claim it is already enabled.

NIC connectivity spans internet, Azure and on-premises resources with VNET policies inherited; the private-boundary prose is not a universal no-internet guarantee. NIC-provisioning include is separately scope-bound.

The diagram caption and six-step textual flow describe workflow trigger, runner creation, NIC deployment, job pickup/queue, service logs and on-premises access. Raster asset is not visually reviewed or native behavior verified.
Azure VNET hosted runners combine managed CI/CD compute with user-controlled runner network policies; external Azure overview is a reference, not source completion.
VNET network policies including ExpressRoute/VPN access and NSG outbound rules apply to runner NICs; runner traffic monitoring depends on network logs being enabled.
Runner outbound behavior follows the network; Azure default outbound IPs are unpredictable and cannot be added to GitHub IP allow lists. Stable-IP guidance is linked, not implemented.

Azure setup precedes GitHub network configuration; FPT links organization instructions, GHEC includes enterprise policy and links both enterprise and organization procedures. Conditional navigation is preserved without certifying linked bodies.

GHEC organization owners may configure organization private networking; non-GHEC branch specifies organization owners on Team. Owner role and plan are explicit applicability limits, not actual permission evidence.

The source announces NICs will soon be provisioned in a service subscription, invisible in user subscriptions but consuming subnet IPs. Forward-looking wording is not current deployment identity or verified transition.

Azure setup calls for Subscription Contributor and Network Contributor for provider registration/subnet delegation, NetworkSettings in the VNET subscription and resources in the same region for availability/residency. No role granted.

Default VMs do not trust TLS interception intermediate certificates, so outbound interception is prohibited in the default case; a custom image installing intermediate certificates is the stated alternative, not a universal interception ban.
DNS/domain controls are recommended using GitHub meta; pinned prose announces previous IP closure on or after July 1, 2026. Date passage alone does not prove live closure.
Meta choices are exact domains.actions_inbound.full_domains, mixed domains.actions and mostly wildcard domains.actions_inbound.wildcard_domains; wildcard stability and precision differ.

Required domains change with at least one week's advance listing and no last-updated timestamp; specific lists require weekly checks and network updates. Minimum basic domains may need additions for use cases, and implementation technology is unspecified.

Static IP Bicep is closing down, unmaintained and retained for migration, with removal on or after July 1, 2026; hard-coding risks breakage. Source recommends 30% subnet capacity buffer (300 concurrency to 390), not universally adopted threshold; data residency adds ingress IP ranges.

Deprecated Bicep uses parameterized location/name and NSG API 2017-06-01; first rule allows outbound TCP 443 to VirtualNetwork at priority 200 from any source address/port. Not a complete security policy.

Two static IPv4 destination datasets allow outbound port 443 with wildcard protocol/source at priorities 210 Actions and 220 GitHub. Every listed address belongs to a deprecated example dataset, not a verified current allow list; spans retain the complete datasets without redistribution of raw source.

Final rule allows outbound 443 to Storage with wildcard protocol/source at priority 230. All four example rules are outbound Allow; no explicit inbound Deny appears, so deploying this example alone would not establish the separate all-inbound-block recommendation.
